title: Open-ended Multi-agent Autocurricula via Visual Inspection of Policies with Multi-modal LLMs

paper.title: Open-ended Multi-agent Autocurricula via Visual Inspection of Policies with Multi-modal LLMs
paper.abstract: Abstract Open-ended curricula in Reinforcement Learning (RL) aim to train generally-capable agents by identifying tasks that facilitate learning increasingly complex skills. A major challenge when designing such curricula is assessing task difficulty relative to the agent’s current learning progress. While previous work has explored using scalar task scores or textual summaries of the agent’s behavior, here we study a different approach: directly inspecting policy behavior via recorded episode videos. We introduce a simple yet effective instantiation of this approach which leverages a Video Language Model (VLM) to both process these videos and provide curriculum recommendations, which we call Visual Inspection of Policies (VIP). Since videos can naturally contain any number of controllable agents, we empirically study VIP on the StarCraft Multi-Agent Challenge (SMAC). We show that even with a lightweight and openly accessible VLM (VideoLLaMa2-7B), VIP can use policy videos to generate more effective curricula than both its text-only ablation and methods that rely on scalar task scores.

A major challenge when designing such curricula is assessing task difficulty relative to the agent’s current learning progress. While previous work has explored using scalar task scores or textual summaries of the agent’s behavior, here we study a different approach: directly inspecting policy behavior via recorded episode videos. We introduce a simple yet effective instantiation of this approach which leverages a Video Language Model (VLM) to both process these videos and provide curriculum recommendations, which we call Visual Inspection of Policies (VIP). Since videos can naturally contain any number of controllable agents, we empirically study VIP on the StarCraft Multi-Agent Challenge (SMAC). We show that even with a lightweight and openly accessible VLM (VideoLLaMa2-7B), VIP can use policy videos to generate more effective curricula than both its text-only ablation and methods that rely on scalar task scores. Figure 1: An example of how policy videos can capture promising curriculum directions that are inaccessible to methods based on learning signal. The four images are selected frames from an episode video recorded in the StarCraft Multi-Agent Challenge (SMAC) environment. While allied troops (green) have obtained a clear numbers advantage with an effective strategy in (a), they still end up losing this match to a single enemy (red) after panicking in (b) and (d). Despite the 0% win rate, agents are close to discovering a winning strategy — notably, this insight is inaccessible to any curriculum curator that relies on local learning signals (e.g. Unsupervised Environment Design ( Dennis et al., 2020 ) ). Here we instead propose a method to harness this information with a Vision Language Model (VLM), which we call Visual Inspection of Policies . In this exact scenario, VIP chooses to continue training on the same task, achieving a substantial improvement to an ∼ \sim 80% win rate. Quantitative results supporting this intuition are reported in Section 5 (text-only ablation); other related qualitative analyses are also reported in Appendix D . 1 Introduction Many real-world Reinforcement Learning (RL) tasks are difficult or impossible to solve by simply starting from a random policy and directly trying to optimize its downstream performance ( Wang et al., 2019 ; Wang et al., 2020a ) . These tasks typically require intermediate “stepping stone” skills that are hard to discover with direct optimization and are impossible to identify in advance without extensive domain knowledge. This has motivated research into methods to automatically design open-ended curricula ( Wang et al., 2020b ; Dennis et al., 2020 ; Zhang et al., 2024a ; Wang et al., 2023 ) which both discover and solve increasingly complex tasks. The ultimate goal of these methods is to produce generally-capable agents that can quickly adapt to any task in a particular domain, including those unseen in training. To this end, the curriculum must recommend tasks that are neither too easy nor too hard, so that the agent is presented with the most interesting task that is still solvable. This tradeoff is typically highly dependent on the current learning progress of the agent: tasks that are easy and uninteresting to a very competent agent might still be worth tackling for an agent which has just started learning. To correctly identify tasks that satisfy these properties, previous work has explored both scalar numerical scores ( Jiang et al., 2021b ; Rutherford et al., 2024 ; Jiang et al., 2021a ) and textual summaries of the agent’s behavior ( Zhang et al., 2024a ; Aki et al., 2024 ) . The former typically estimate the learning signal that a task could provide, which can be limiting when the reward signal is sparse or deceptive. Many multi-agent games, for example, provide both a sparse reward signal (win rate) and heuristic dense rewards (e.g. eliminating opponents) to aid exploration. However, since these heuristic rewards are not always correlated with winning strategies, relying solely on the learning signal can fail to recognize policies that are close to discovering successful strategies, as shown in Figure 1 . Determining learning potential with text-only summaries ( Zhang et al., 2024a ; Wang et al., 2023 ) is limited for the same reason. Moreover, these approaches typically build on the human-like priors of LLMs to choose interesting tasks; however, a human in the same position would typically rely on visual cues by observing the agent’s behavior directly. A sports coach, for example, would much rather review the video of a match rather than only read descriptions of an athlete’s performance. Nonetheless, this more direct visual approach has been inaccessible to RL autocurricula until the recent breakthrough of multi-modal LLMs and, more specifically, VLMs. Contributions We bridge the gap discussed above by introducing a new approach to open-ended autocurricula: Visual Inspection of Policies (VIP), outlined in Figure 2 . VIP directly feeds episode videos of the current policy to a Vision Language Model (VLM) to gain direct access to visual information that might be missing in numerical or textual summaries. Additionally, VIP is independent of the number of agents in the environment as long as they are rendered in the same video. We apply VIP to the popular StarCraft Multi-Agent Challenge (SMAC), a complex, strategic, multi-agent collaborative domain with varying number and types of agents, previously unexplored in unsupervised RL autocurricula. We find that VIP outperforms other autocurricula based on learning signal, and that episode videos play a crucial role in its effectiveness. Figure 2: An overview of Visual Inspection of Policies (VIP). At each step of the curriculum, the agent is trained on the current task with a (Multi-Agent) Reinforcement Learning algorithm. Then, one or more recordings of episodes from the current policy are fed to the VLM, alongside a small textual summary of the agent’s performance (e.g. win rate). The VLM is prompted to recommend the next interesting task, based on its assessment of the current capabilities of the agent. Finally, the raw recommendation from the VLM is compared with the set of tasks available to the curriculum (task space) using a sentence similarity module, to make sure the task is a valid specification. 2 Related work Automatic Curriculum Learning Open-ended autocurricula in Reinforcement Learning have their roots in Automatic Curriculum Learning (ACL). Standard ACL methods are supervised: they target a single final task and design a curriculum tailored to that task. Wang et al. (2020b) generates curricula in multi-agent environments by progressively incrementing the number of agents. PORTAL ( Wu et al., 2023 ) is another multi-agent ACL method which constructs the curriculum by evaluating the similarity between intermediate tasks. STAR-MARL ( Li et al., 2026 ) adopts an LLM to automatically generate appropriate sub-task trees from a known downstream MARL task. Open-Ended Autocurricula In contrast to supervised ACL, open-ended autocurricula are fully unsupervised and do not target a single final task, assuming no knowledge on the identity, number or other properties of the downstream tasks. Open-ended autocurricula explicitly aim to continually propose worthwhile tasks to the learning agent and are closely related to the adjacent fields of lifelong learning and Continual Reinforcement Learning ( Abel et al., 2023 ) . A popular way to automatically design open-ended curricula is leveraging evolutionary computation methods, such as in POET and enhanced-POET ( Wang et al., 2019 ; Wang et al., 2020a ) : these co-evolve populations of agents and environments in a divergent process to discover and solve novel problems indefinitely. While highly influential, these works do not provide a clear mechanism for reusing the knowledge acquired by the agent population on unseen tasks, require substantial computational resources, and cannot be easily extended to multi-agent settings. Unsupervised Environment Design Unsupervised Environment Design (UED) ( Dennis et al., 2020 ) is a more recent framework for open-ended curriculum generation based on minimax regret optimization. UED has been implemented both in teacher-student algorithms ( Dennis et al., 2020 ; Jiang et al., 2021a ) and in autocurricula based on estimates of learning potential ( Jiang et al., 2021b ; Jiang et al., 2021a ; Parker-Holder et al., 2022 ) . Recent work has studied how these estimates might be vulnerable to selecting tasks that are too hard ( Rutherford et al., 2024 ) , suggesting an alternative for boolean-outcome deterministic tasks. While these methods are designed for single-agent domains, UED has also been applied to multi-agent settings with MAESTRO ( Samvelyan et al., 2023 ) . However, MAESTRO is designed for two-player, adversarial, zero-sum games, and is not applicable to domains with higher or variable number of agents. LLM-Guided Autocurricula The breakthrough of LLMs provided a new means to automatically design open-ended curricula, both to evaluate agent progress and propose new tasks. LLM-POET ( Aki et al., 2024 ) combines LLMs with the POET algorithm discussed above. OMNI and OMNI-EPIC ( Zhang et al., 2024a ; Faldor et al., 2025 ) employ the LLM as model of interest (MOI) biased towards tasks at the frontier of the agent capabilities that would also be interesting to a human. OMNI-EPIC also experiments with Video LMs but finds them to not be sufficiently reliable. However, their use of Video LMs is relegated to the role of success detectors, again falling into the bucket of compressing rich behaviors into brief summaries. Moreover, OMNI-EPIC relies on the domain exposing a way to program environments in code, which is realistically verified only for simulations that feature such functionality. For example, OMNI-EPIC cannot be applied to any simulation benchmark where physics and/or world dynamics are not properly decoupled from environment variants. Dharna et al. (2025) propose a method that combines the power of the human priors contained in Foundation Models (FMs) with self-play. This method, however, scales with the number of agents and is not trivially extensible to variable or high number of agents. Zhang et al. (2024b) propose a method with some similarities to VIP, which uses a VLM to guide open-ended RL training experiments, including recommending intermediate tasks in a curriculum. However, this method relies on manually identifying a set of skills before the start of the learning process, requiring significant prior domain knowledge and manual design. Positioning All of the approaches discussed above use aggregate information on the current learning progress to choose the next best task. Scalar task scoring such as in UED might fail to capture nuanced information that is not directly linked to learning signals — on the other hand, LLM-based methods mostly focus on describing the candidate tasks, rather than describing the learning progress of the current policy.
